title: India's Factory Growth Just Hit a Near Four-Year Low — and the Warning Signs Go Beyond One Bad Month
excerpt: The HSBC India Manufacturing PMI fell to 54.2 in June as new orders, exports, and hiring all lost momentum — raising questions about whether the post-pandemic industrial boom is finally cooling.
body:
India's manufacturing sector expanded at its second-slowest pace since mid-2022 in June, as demand for goods softened across the board and hiring growth dropped to its weakest level this year. The data, released Wednesday by S&P Global, paints a picture of an industrial economy that remains in expansion territory but is losing steam at an uncomfortable pace.

The HSBC India Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 54.2 in June from 55.0 in May, slightly below the preliminary estimate of 54.5. Only March's reading was weaker in the past four years. A reading above 50 indicates expansion — but the direction of travel matters as much as the absolute number.

## Where the Slowdown Is Showing

New orders — the single most important forward-looking component of the survey — grew at their second-weakest rate since June 2022. This came after a three-month high in May, suggesting the demand recovery that followed the easing of Middle East tensions may have been shorter-lived than investors hoped.

The export picture is more concerning. International sales grew at their weakest pace in 39 months, with firms specifically citing subdued demand from European clients. For an economy that has been positioning itself as a manufacturing alternative to China, that's a data point worth watching.

"The moderation suggests demand has cooled slightly after the earlier surge linked to the Middle East conflict," said Pranjul Bhandari, Chief India Economist at HSBC. "Growth slowed across output, new orders, export orders and employment, with international sales recording their weakest increase since March 2023."

## The Jobs Signal

Perhaps the most consequential number in the report is the employment reading. Hiring expanded at its weakest pace in 2026 so far, with a striking 97 percent of firms keeping headcount unchanged, citing adequate capacity. Manufacturing is widely considered India's biggest job multiplier — when factories stop hiring, the downstream effects ripple through transport, logistics, and services.

The reluctance to hire is consistent with the broader demand picture. Backlogs of work were broadly unchanged, suggesting firms aren't struggling to keep up with orders — they're worried about whether the next round of orders will come.

## A Silver Lining in Prices

The one unambiguously positive signal in the data is on inflation. Both input and output price indices declined, pointing to softer cost pressures as the geopolitical disruptions that drove commodity prices higher earlier this year begin to recede.

Output charges rose at their slowest rate in three months, with 93 percent of companies leaving prices unchanged from May. Input cost inflation eased to a four-month low, though firms continued to flag elevated prices for chemicals, metals, petroleum products, and plastics.

For the Reserve Bank of India, which cut rates in April and has been signalling openness to further easing, the combination of softer demand and retreating inflation may provide the justification for another move. The central bank's next policy meeting is in August.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

The PMI data arrives at a delicate moment for Indian equities. The Sensex and Nifty posted monthly gains in June — up 2.3 percent and 1.4 percent respectively — buoyed by falling oil prices, a stabilising rupee, and record foreign inflows into government bonds. But factory data like this tests the sustainability of that rally.

Capital goods — the segment that reflects industrial investment — was the sole driver of the slowdown, with a notable fall in growth rates while consumer and intermediate goods actually accelerated. That divergence matters: it suggests corporate India may be pulling back on expansion spending even as consumer demand holds.

For NRI investors with exposure to Indian manufacturing, auto, and industrial stocks, the next data point to watch is the June services PMI, due Friday. India's services sector has consistently outperformed manufacturing, and a strong services reading could offset some of the factory-side weakness. But if services follow manufacturing lower, the narrative shifts from a temporary cool-off to something more structural.

Business confidence fell to a five-month low in June. The proportion of firms forecasting output growth in the year ahead halved since May. That's not panic — but it's prudence, and prudence in Indian industry has a way of becoming self-fulfilling.

**Sources:** S&P Global / HSBC India Manufacturing PMI (July 1, 2026); The Hindu BusinessLine; Reuters; BSE/NSE market data.
